This is the **performance companion** to the [wall-bounded turbulence example](../../examples/wall-bounded-turbulence/index.qmd),
which is about *reproducing* the Moser–Kim–Mansour 1999 channel-flow statistics. Here we answer a
different question: **how efficiently does `peclet.flow` run that DNS across many GPUs of the Snellius
supercomputer?**

## What we measure

The right scaling metric for a production DNS is **weak scaling** — hold the work *per GPU* fixed and
grow the problem with the GPU count. It answers the question you actually have: *"can I run a
proportionally bigger (finer / larger-box) DNS on more GPUs in the same wall-clock?"* We fix **46 M
cells per GPU** (the production $\Delta^+=1.5$ cross-section, $240\times503$, growing the streamwise
extent with the GPU count) and sweep 1 → 8 H100s.

All runs use the **GPU-aware MPI** halo (device pointers handed straight to MPI via a CUDA-aware
UCX/OpenMPI stack), one MPI rank cgroup-bound to each GPU, on Snellius' `gpu_h100` partition.

## Results

![Weak scaling on Snellius H100 (46 M cells/GPU fixed). On-node scaling is near-ideal; the drop from 4→8 GPUs is the inter-node pressure-solve reduction tax.](weak_scaling.png)

| GPUs | nodes | box | cells | ms/step | weak-scaling eff. | throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | $377\times240\times503$ | 46 M | 1369 | 100 % | 33 Mcell/s |
| 2 | 1 | $754\times240\times503$ | 91 M | 1300 | **105 %** | 70 Mcell/s |
| 4 | 1 | $1508\times240\times503$ | **182 M** | 1713 | **80 %** | 106 Mcell/s |
| 8 | 2 | $3016\times240\times503$ | 364 M | 2942 | 47 % | 124 Mcell/s |

**On a single node, scaling is near-ideal.** Two GPUs is even marginally *faster* per step than one —
the intra-node `cuda_ipc` halo exchange is essentially free — and the full **182 M production run on 4
GPUs holds 80 % weak efficiency**. That is the sweet spot for one converged DNS: big enough per GPU to
stay compute-bound, single-node so it pays no inter-node communication.

**Crossing to a second node (8 GPUs) drops efficiency to ~47 %.** This is expected physics, not a
defect: the incompressible **pressure Poisson solve does a global all-reduce every Krylov iteration**,
and once those reductions travel over InfiniBand they become latency-bound. Communication-light coarse
solves (an agglomerated bottom, a reduction-free Chebyshev accelerator) are the suite's active at-scale
frontier — but for a single production DNS the 4-GPU single-node point already delivers it in ~a day.

Reproduce with [`weak_scaling.sh`](../../examples/wall-bounded-turbulence/weak_scaling.sh) (and the
strong-scaling counterpart [`scaling_test.sh`](../../examples/wall-bounded-turbulence/scaling_test.sh));
the figure is regenerated by [`plot_scaling.py`](plot_scaling.py).

## The fix that made the large runs possible

The 182 M-on-4-GPU run initially **crashed** with `cudaErrorIllegalAddress`. It is worth recording how
it was found and fixed, because it is a representative example of debugging a device + MPI code at scale.

**Symptom.** Distributed-only (single-rank of the same 46 M problem was fine), CUDA-only, and
*nondeterministic* across rank counts — 8 ranks ran the same block that 2 and 4 ranks crashed on.

**Diagnosis.** The failure was reproduced at *tiny* scale (a $132\times32\times131$ box, 2 ranks sharing
one GPU) under `compute-sanitizer`, which named the kernel: `prolongAdd`, reading out of bounds. Root
cause, confirmed in the code: the distributed cut-cell **pressure multigrid decomposed each level with
an independent ORB**, so coarse blocks did not *nest* in fine ones. When coarsening changes the longest
axis — here $x$ halves ($754\to377$) while $z=503$ is odd and cannot coarsen, so $z$ becomes longest and
the coarse level splits **z** where the fine level split **x** — the restrict/prolong transfers (which
assume coarse-local $i \leftrightarrow$ fine-local $2i$) read across the misaligned block boundary. At
small per-rank blocks the overrun stays in mapped memory (garbage, no fault); at large blocks it crosses
into an unmapped page → the illegal-address crash.

**Fix** (peclet `core` + `flow`): build each coarse level as the fine decomposition **coarsened in
place** — an aligned ORB (split positions snapped to powers of two) plus a `coarsened()` derivation that
divides the block layout, preserving rank order. Coarse blocks then nest by construction, so
restrict/prolong stay purely local (no added communication). Verified: the reproduction goes from 7
sanitizer errors to **0**, the distributed result is **bit-exact to single-rank** ($\max|\Delta U|\approx
4\times10^{-14}$), and the full `flow` (33/33) and `dem` (24/24) MPI test suites stay green.

Everything needed to run this on Snellius — a source build with the GPU-aware 2024a toolchain, the
one-GPU-per-rank binding, the SBU accounting, and the job scripts — is documented in the
